client: I got a really low grade on my final project last week, and it's been messing with my head ever since. I keep thinking maybe I'm just not smart enough to be in this program, like maybe I've been fooling everyone including myself this whole time. I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It means a lot that you decided to give this a shot, even when you're feeling doubtful — that takes real courage. That thought, "I've been fooling everyone including myself," sounds incredibly heavy to carry, and I can understand why one grade would shake your confidence so deeply when you care this much about your work. I'm curious — when you look back at your journey in this program *before* this grade, what evidence do you see that either supports or challenges the idea that you don't belong here?

client: I mean, I guess there have been some good moments — I got decent grades on a couple of earlier assignments, and one professor even commented that my analysis was "thoughtful." But when I think about those things now, they just feel like flukes, like maybe the bar was lower or I got lucky somehow. It's hard to hold onto those as real evidence when this one bad grade feels so much more true about who I actually am.
therapist: What you're describing has a name in CBT — it's called "discounting the positives," where our mind convinces us that good evidence doesn't really count, while negative evidence feels like the absolute truth. It's worth noticing that you're not applying the same skeptical lens to the bad grade — you're not wondering if *that* was a fluke, or if the feedback was incomplete, or if something else was going on. What do you think it says about you that your mind is so quick to protect the negative interpretation and dismiss the positive ones?

client: That's an interesting way to frame it, but honestly it feels a little too neat, like slapping a label on it somehow makes it easier to dismiss what I'm actually feeling. I get what you're saying about the double standard, but the low grade feels more real because it's recent and concrete, whereas the earlier stuff already faded. I guess I'm just not sure that knowing there's a name for this pattern is going to make it stop.
therapist: You're absolutely right to push back on that — naming a pattern doesn't make the pain of that grade any less real, and I don't want you to feel like I'm handing you a concept to skip past what you're actually experiencing. What you said about recency is really important though — I'm wondering if the grade feels more "true" right now partly because the wound is still fresh, rather than because it's actually more accurate than all that earlier evidence. What do you think it would take for one of those positive moments — like your professor's comment — to feel just as real and recent to you as this grade does right now?

client: Honestly, I'm not sure anything would make it feel as real — and that's kind of what scares me. Like, I could try to remind myself of that professor's comment, but it would feel forced, like I'm just trying to talk myself into something I don't actually believe. I think part of me is worried that if I let myself feel good about those moments, I'm just setting myself up to be blindsided again like I was with this grade.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense — if good feelings just become ammunition for a harder fall later, why risk it at all? What you're describing sounds less like a thinking problem and more like a protective strategy your mind has developed, where staying in the low place feels safer than hoping and being disappointed again. I'm wondering, though — how is that protection actually working out for you day to day; is staying guarded from hope making you feel safer, or is it costing you something too?

client: Honestly, it's costing me a lot — I've been avoiding working on my next assignment because I'm already convinced it won't go well, and I've been kind of withdrawing from people in my program because I don't want them to see me struggling. But even knowing that, I don't know how to just switch off the guardedness, it's not like I can decide to stop protecting myself and suddenly feel okay with the risk of hoping again.
therapist: You're absolutely right that you can't just flip a switch on something that's been protecting you — and I want to be clear that I'm not asking you to. But I notice something important: the guardedness that was meant to protect you is now actually creating the outcomes you're afraid of, where avoiding the assignment and withdrawing from peers is quietly building a case *for* the story that you don't belong. What if, instead of trying to feel hopeful, we just focused on one tiny action — not to prove anything, but just to gently interrupt that pattern — what would the smallest possible step toward that next assignment look like for you?

client: Maybe just opening the document and reading the prompt, without actually having to write anything yet — that feels like something I could maybe do without it turning into a spiral. But I'm already thinking about how even that small thing might make me feel worse, like once I see the prompt I'll be confronted with how behind I am and it'll confirm everything I've been telling myself. I guess I'm just not sure a small step actually changes the bigger feeling underneath it all.
therapist: That's a really honest and self-aware observation — you're not just agreeing to the small step, you're already thinking through what could go wrong, and that tells me you're taking this seriously rather than just telling me what I want to hear. You're right that opening a document won't magically dissolve the bigger fear underneath, but I'd gently offer that the goal isn't to feel better *before* you open it — it's just to collect some real information about what actually happens, rather than letting your mind's prediction go unchallenged. If you did open it and it *did* feel hard, what do you think that would actually mean — and is that different from what it would mean if you avoided it entirely?

client: I guess if I opened it and it felt hard, that would just mean the work is hard — it wouldn't necessarily mean I'm not capable of doing it, even though my brain would probably try to make it mean that. And yeah, avoiding it entirely is kind of worse in a way, because at least if I try I have something real to work with instead of just this dread I've been sitting with. I'm still not fully convinced this is going to shift anything, but I can see the logic in what you're saying, even if feeling it is a different thing entirely.
therapist: That distinction you just made — between the work being hard and *you* being incapable — is genuinely significant, and you arrived at that yourself, which matters more than if I had just handed it to you. You're also naming something really true: that knowing something logically and feeling it are two different things, and that gap doesn't close overnight, it closes slowly through small moments of real experience that start to build a different kind of evidence. So I want to ask — not as a homework assignment, but just out of curiosity — when might you give yourself a chance to open that document, and what would you want to notice about what actually happens versus what your mind predicted would happen?

client: Maybe tonight, when I get home and it's quiet — that feels more realistic than saying "right now" and then not following through. I think what I'd want to notice is whether the dread actually gets worse once I open it, or whether it stays the same or even levels off a little, because my mind is predicting total overwhelm and maybe that's worth testing. I'm still a bit nervous that I'll open it, feel awful, and then use that as more evidence against myself, but I guess that's kind of the thing we've been talking about — whether I can catch myself doing that in the moment.
therapist: That plan sounds genuinely thoughtful — choosing tonight when it's quiet shows you know yourself well enough to set yourself up for success rather than just making a promise that doesn't fit your reality. And the fact that you're already anticipating the trap — that feeling awful might become more "evidence" — means part of you is ready to be a fair witness to yourself rather than just a harsh judge. When you do open it tonight, and your mind starts to interpret what you're feeling, I wonder if you could ask yourself one question: "Am I observing what's actually happening, or am I just confirming what I already decided was true?"

client: That question actually feels like something I could hold onto, because it's not asking me to feel differently, it's just asking me to slow down and check what's actually happening versus what I'm assuming. I think the hard part will be remembering to ask it in the moment when I'm already in my head and the anxiety is loud — it's easy to think clearly about this stuff now, but a lot harder when I'm sitting alone with the document open in front of me. I guess I just hope I don't forget all of this the second things get difficult tonight.
therapist: It's really meaningful that the question resonates with you, and you're being honest about something important — insight in a calm moment and access to that insight when anxiety is loud are genuinely different challenges, not a personal failing. One small thing that might help bridge that gap: before you open the document tonight, you could take just a moment to write that question down somewhere you'll actually see it, so it's there waiting for you rather than something you have to remember under pressure. And whatever happens tonight — whether it goes smoothly or gets hard — I'd love to hear what you noticed; what do you think you'll take away from this conversation as you head into the rest of your day?

client: I think what I'm taking away is that I've been treating this one grade like it's the final verdict on everything, and maybe it doesn't have to be that — even if part of me still wants to argue that it is. Writing the question down actually seems doable in a way that doesn't feel like too much pressure, which I appreciate because a lot of what gets suggested in these kinds of conversations feels like it requires more energy than I have right now. I'm still not sure how tonight will go, but I feel a little less alone with it than I did when I walked in here, and I guess that's something.
therapist: That last part — feeling a little less alone with it — is not a small thing, and I want you to really let that land rather than brush past it. You came in skeptical, you pushed back when something didn't feel right, and you still did the hard work of thinking honestly about what's actually going on — that's not nothing, that's exactly the kind of thoughtfulness your professor noticed in you. Go easy on yourself tonight, and whatever happens with that document, remember that one evening's experience is just one more piece of evidence — not a verdict.
